name: critical-thinking
title: Critical thinking
scope: A study card for judging a claim by its evidence, assumptions, alternatives, and named fallacies.
method: Restate the claim in neutral words.
List the evidence that was actually offered.
Name the assumption the argument needs.
Name a fallacy only if the reasoning matches it.
State the conclusion strength and what evidence is still missing.

formulas.name: Claim
formulas.use: Restate it so the maker would recognize it.

formulas.name: Evidence
formulas.expr: The observation or source offered for the claim.
formulas.use: Keep evidence separate from the conclusion drawn from it.

formulas.name: Assumption
formulas.expr: An unstated idea the argument needs in order to work.
formulas.use: Name it explicitly before judging the conclusion.

formulas.name: Alternative
formulas.expr: Another explanation that also fits the evidence.
formulas.use: A live alternative lowers confidence even when the original claim is possible.

formulas.name: Ad hominem
formulas.expr: Attacking the person instead of the claim.
formulas.use: An insult is not a rebuttal, though a relevant conflict of interest can still bear on the source.

formulas.name: Straw man
formulas.expr: Misrepresenting a position, then attacking that misrepresentation.
formulas.use: Compare the restatement with what was actually said.

formulas.name: False dilemma
formulas.expr: Treating two options as the only options.
formulas.use: Ask what other choices or mixed positions were left out.

formulas.name: Hasty generalization
formulas.expr: Drawing a broad rule from too few or unrepresentative cases.
formulas.use: Ask how many cases were seen and whether they were selected fairly.

formulas.name: Appeal to authority
formulas.expr: Treating a citation as proof when expertise or evidence is missing.
formulas.use: A relevant expert is a lead, not a substitute for the evidence itself.

formulas.name: Correlation is not causation
formulas.expr: Two things varying together do not by themselves show that one causes the other.
formulas.use: A correlation can suggest a hypothesis; it does not identify the cause.

checks: The restated claim matches what was actually said.
Evidence is listed separately from the conclusion.
The alternative could still fit the same evidence.
A named fallacy matches its definition, not merely a disliked conclusion.
limits: Naming a fallacy does not prove the conclusion is false.
This card does not replace evidence from the subject itself.
Conclusion strength judges the argument, not the person.
